### Contributing guidelines

- [x] I have read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] I have read [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Module(s)

mini.keymap

### Description

Please leave your feedback about new [mini.keymap](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/readmes/mini-keymap.md) module here. Feel free to either add new comment or positively upvote existing one.

Some things I am interested to find out (obviously, besides bugs):

- What built-in steps for [`map_multistep()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ee23e1abc206efc6d6cce19ec8c0a3da7a897035/doc/mini-keymap.txt#L220-L261) that are currently missing would you find useful? They probably have to be convenient to use as one of `<Tab>` / `<S-Tab>` / `<CR>` / `<BS>` key in Insert mode.
- Is configuration of common mappings intuitive enough?
- Is documentation and examples clear enough?

Thanks!

I'm starting to get it a little.

If I understand correctly, `map_combo` keymaps behave *almost* the same way as `<nowait>` keymaps but allow for controlling the exact delay per mapping.

```lua

--
local map_combo = require('mini.keymap').map_combo

```

I very much like the new module!

The smart snippet mappings are also useful when not using `tab`:

```lua
local mappings = nil
if MiniKeymap then
  local map_multistep = MiniKeymap.map_multistep
  local next_or_out = { "minisnippets_next", "jump_after_tsnode", "jump_after_close" }
  map_multistep("i", "<C-l>", next_or_out)

  local prev_or_out = { "minisnippets_prev", "jump_before_tsnode", "jump_before_open" }
  map_multistep("i", "<C-h>", prev_or_out)

  mappings = { jump_next = "", jump_prev = "" } -- already defined above...
end

mini_snippets.setup({
  -- ...
  mappings = mappings,
  -- ...
})


```

> If I understand correctly, `map_combo` keymaps behave the same way as `<nowait>` keymaps but allow for controlling the exact delay per mapping.

Not quite. The whole reason for this "better escape" like approaches to mappings is the behavior of the cursor when typing initial keys from the left hand side:
- With regular mappings there is a visible visual delay for a duration of 'timeoutlen' during which Neovim waits for the next key.
- With combos (and "better escape" like approaches) there is no such side effects.

Plus, there can be several combos for the same LHS.

> The smart snippet mappings are also useful when not using `tab`:

Yeah, that's also possible of course.

---

I saw your comment on Reddit :) It would have been pushed to `main` at the time you commented here, but there were some test fails on Nightly.

On latest `main` the `jump_{before,after}_tsnode` built-in steps now [only require active parser](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/473cdbff498ed120f1768c75ef65fa42859aa14f/doc/mini-keymap.txt#L245-L246), i.e. work in any mode. But beware that the actual cursor placement might be not ideal for Normal/Visual mode: it is placed at the same position at which it is placed in Insert mode. This means that `jump_before_tsnode` places exactly on node start while `jump_after_tsnode` places just after node end.

Everything works *exactly* as expected here. There is `["<Esc>"] = { "cancel", "fallback" }` special mapping in 'blink.cmp' which is responsible for this behavior. The combo mimics `<BS><BS><Esc>` as if typed by the user, which in this case doesn't exit into Normal mode if there are suggestions from 'blink.cmp'. You can see it by manually typing `jk<BS><BS><Esc>` without created combo.

One workaround is to use something like this:

```lua
local map_combo = require("mini.keymap").map_combo
map_combo({ "i", "t" }, "jk", "<BS><BS><Cmd>stopinsert<CR>", { delay = 150 })
map_combo({ "c", "s" }, "jk", "<BS><BS><Esc>", { delay = 150 })
map_combo("t", "jk", "<BS><BS><C-\\><C-n>", { delay = 150 })
map_combo("n", "jk", "<cmd>wincmd =<cr>k", { delay = 150 })
```

Would it be possible to make `jump_{before,after}_{close,open}` work in Normal mode as well?

My current setup is [in-and-out.nvim](https://github.com/ysmb-wtsg/in-and-out.nvim) in Normal mode and [neotab.nvim](https://github.com/kawre/neotab.nvim) in Insert. Can't remember exactly why but it works for me and I'd like to use `mini.keymap` to replace both.

> Would it be possible to make `jump_{before,after}_{close,open}` work in Normal mode as well?

Those are specifically targeted for Insert mode because it requires custom cursor adjustment to work in more edge cases. I did try to only use `search()` flags, but they didn't work for some `after_close` cases (see [these notes](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/51cec14696190ad5b61e6c559ae558c703b71906/lua/mini/keymap.lua#L425-L431) and [this commit's message](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/commit/3a605ad16f2e4a79866a0a81dce963243e92ed5c)).

After thinking a bit, I realized that only `jump_before_open` and `jump_after_close` need to be conditioned on Insert mode. The `gen_step.search_pattern` does not. So it now works in any mode on latest `main`. See [this example](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/6105b69d79fef0afed5ed576081b1997ef2b4be1/doc/mini-keymap.txt#L370-L380) on how to set up in not only Insert mode.

Okay, I think it's a stupid idea, but is it even possible to perform a `map_combo` action on a completion menu (in my case `blink.cmp`)?
Plugins have their own autocmds to trigger and they change the completion menu as soon as the first key is pressed.

> Okay, I think it's a stupid idea, but is it even possible to perform a `map_combo` action on a completion menu (in my case `blink.cmp`)?

A combo abstraction by itself is not tied to conditions (like "there is active completion menu"). That can be checked inside its callable action.

But yes, when it comes to interacting with some other plugin that itself provides interactive features, there might be issues with it not properly "registering" keystrokes used by the combo to emulate its action.

I think this is a wonderful feature that shows a lot of potential.

I'm using features like:

```lua
map_combo({ 'i', 'c' }, 'dp', '<bs><bs><esc>dip')
map_combo({ 'i', 'c' }, 'pd', '<bs><bs><esc>dip')
```

and they are really convenient.

I have a question about how to use it more effectively:

When I set it up like this:

```lua
map_combo({ 'n', 'x' }, 'dp', 'dip')
map_combo({ 'n', 'x' }, 'pd', 'dip')
```

it doesn't work as intended.
This is because the 'd' in 'dp' deletes the text at that point.
Is there a way to configure it to prevent 'dp' from actually being typed?

> I have a question about how to use it more effectively:
> 
> When I set it up like this:
> 
> ```lua
> map_combo({ 'n', 'x' }, 'dp', 'dip')
> map_combo({ 'n', 'x' }, 'pd', 'dip')
> ```
> 
> it doesn't work as intended. This is because the 'd' in 'dp' deletes the text at that point. Is there a way to configure it to prevent 'dp' from actually being typed?

This is an intended behavior of a combo: each key is executed uninterrupted while there is some side effect if they all are typed within certain amount delay between each other. If you want to have "dp" actually mean "dip", use regular mappings (`vim.keymap.set`).
